title: A Proposal for Saving Five Million Hours per Year (One Day per Teacher) of Workload, Without Harming Pupil Achievement per-teacher-of-workload-without-harming-pupil-achievement/
author: Sam Sims
source: Sam Sims Quantitative Education Research (samsims.education), April 25, 2024
summary: Sam Sims argues that the widespread practice of half-termly 'data drop' testing to track pupil progress and target interventions is built on statistical noise. Drawing on FFT Datalab data and an EEF review of measurement error, he shows that for the vast majority of pupils, a term-to-term change in standardised test scores cannot be distinguished from pure measurement error with any confidence -- only about 5-7% of pupils show a change large enough to be reliably detected, and the true figure is likely even lower given less-precise in-house tests. Since England already has some of the highest teacher working hours among TALIS-surveyed countries, Sims calculates that moving all schools from half-termly to termly data drops would save roughly 1.8 million hours of workload nationally, and moving to a single annual drop would save nearly 5 million hours -- over a full working day per teacher per year -- with no material risk to pupil outcomes.
points: The core statistical finding: based on EEF measurement-error data, only about 5-7% of pupils show a term-to-term test score change large enough to be distinguished from pure measurement error with 90% confidence.

Sims argues this makes most data-drop-triggered 'interventions' a response to random noise rather than genuine pupil decline -- 'we have been allocating pupils to interventions based very largely on random noise.'
England already has some of the highest teacher working hours among TALIS-surveyed countries, and half-termly data collection was recommended against as far back as a 2018 government report.
His back-of-envelope calculation: moving all schools to one annual data drop would save about 4.95 million hours of teacher workload nationally per year -- over a full working day per teacher.
quotes: Most pupils move very little. On a scale where two thirds of pupils score between 85 and 115, half of pupils’ Spring term scores are within 5 points of their Autumn term score.
When we look at the change across one term (the top two graphs), only about one in twenty (5-7%) see a fall in test scores that can be detected with a well-designed test.

We have not encountered any examples of schools where the actions arising after a half termly deposit of attainment data justify the time investment required by teachers to facilitate six data collection points a year.
But when it comes to capturing pupil-level change from one term to the next, termly testing is only informative for a very small minority of pupils.
Across all three groups, this amounts to a saving of 4.95m hours of workload per year, which is just over one day per year (8.7 hours) for every teacher in the country.
